evidence: Task registrations are only logged to console stdout; an operator auditing a machine a week later has no persistent record of what was registered, when, with what commands.
When creating a tracker item takes several seconds, operators cannot tell whether migration, SQLite append, or rendering consumed the time.
The item is stored and returned.
The create endpoint emits no stage timings.
A wave agent with a missing start time has a null duration in the timeline API.
The dashboard's elapsed-time cell and accessible phase title both display the string `nulls` to operators.
The API defines null as an unknown duration.
The test runner partitions modules round-robin without balancing shards by recorded runtime or exporting per-module elapsed times.
This makes it difficult for maintainers to tune how long each shard takes.
The fleet timeline serializes a timezone-aware UTC timestamp and then appends Z.
The browser receives a +00:00Z suffix, Date parsing produces Invalid Date.
The positions of live agents' bars become NaN.
A backup cycle wrote its heartbeat only when it finished. Repository discovery blocked for 22 minutes.
Throughout that window the monitor saw an old heartbeat, and the five-minute scheduler could not start another instance.
The status command reads the repository-local state directory without any environment override.
It reports both heartbeats missing while the shared conductor state contains a recent watchdog heartbeat.
Healthcheck reads the heartbeat from the shared conductor state.
With the conductor root unset, the watchdog dashboard selects a sibling directory containing a sweep log.
It displays STALE while the daemon continues updating its heartbeat under the user's conductor directory.
The merge tools do not provide a per-PR contention report for analysis, requiring operators to manually retrieve PR histories and reconstruct CI attempts, fix rounds, and contended files.
Wave journals contain item timing records, but operators have to manually calculate p50 and p95 and estimate orchestration overhead themselves.
There is no consolidated breakdown, which suggests a need for improvement in the system's ability to provide this information automatically.
FINDING: An operator can inspect token spending against a wave ceiling, but cannot obtain an end-of-wave spending forecast or an early threshold alert from those measurements.
Six writer threads share an event store, which can lead to concurrent access issues.
With the configured one-millisecond SQLite busy window, concurrent appends raise raw database-is-locked errors.
The existing multiwriter test reproduced lost appends in three runs, indicating a real defect.
Creating a tracker item appends the durable event before rendering tracker.json.
When rendering raises WriteConflict, repeating the documented create call mints a second ID.
The next projection contains two copies of the requested item.
Four tracker records were written directly to disk.
The consistency check then refused every projection render.
174 already accepted creation events were absent from tracker.json.
Operators had no supported way to reconcile the records.
The finding states that task lifecycle events can be read from the brain's JSONL file, but it does not provide enough context to determine if this is a defect or an enhancement opportunity.

The finding also mentions that an operator querying the tracker SQLite store must obtain these events separately to join them to other streams, but it does not specify if this is a problem or a requirement.
Operators who want to use Gemini as the worker cannot select it in the Aesop configuration.
The configured worker backends are available, but using this provider requires a new driver and trial runner.
